newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: US railroad boss bullish after Guatemala rail sale.
newsitem.headline: US railroad boss bullish after Guatemala rail sale.

text.p: A U.S. company has won the bid to run Guatemala's deteriorating railway system for an initial investment of $10 million.

"We are attempting to wake it (the rail system) up from its slumber," Henry Posner III, chairman of the Railroad Development Corp of Pittsburgh, told Reuters on Monday. "More to the point, we feel that we owe it to Guatemala to do our best to re-establish rail service and to restore it to its rightful position in the Guatemalan economy."

In a telephone interview Posner expressed optimism about Guatemala as an investment opportunity, despite a history of civil war that ended after 36 years on December 29. On Friday his company beat out another firm to win a 50-year exclusive concession to run Guatemala's railroad lines.

"Railroad Development Corp has done business all over the world from Argentina to Pakistan," Posner said. "We feel that the railroad business is inherently risky politically, but to date we have found more political risk in the state of New York than we have found in the country of Guatemala."

Immediate plans are to restore the Atlantic corridor from Guatemala City to Puerto Barrios, which requires the smallest initial capital investment -- about $10 million -- and is the main short-term traffic opportunity for the railway.

"As that traffic grows and we have some experience under our belts, we will then proceed to reopen the Pacific side," Posner said. "After that we will have to take a hard look at the cost of connecting the Pacific to the Atlantic."

The railroad has not been operated for nearly two years. The 504-mile (813 km) right of way is washed out in places and inhabited by squatters, Posner said. Two working locomotives remain. Former customers all have invested in truck transportation.

Nevertheless, Posner said his company is banking on the long-term viability of the market for railroad freight transportation for sugar, coffee, fuels, fertilizer, steamboat containers, steel products, scrap metal and other products traditionally moved by rail.
The company will pay the government five percent of income in the first two years and 10 percent in the remaining 48.

Its commitment to Guatemala dovetails with President Alvaro Arzu's peacetime agenda and its emphasis on international investment and privatization. The railroad is the first institution to be privatized in program that targets 16 government-run services this year and could hit 56 in all.
